# Playbook: Personal Projects and Open Source

Last verified: 2026-10-29 against the QEMU, Linux kernel and Ghostty policy pages, GitHub's commit-signing docs, and Claude Code's settings reference. Demo re-run on macOS the same day.

Starts from: nothing; terms are defined on first use.
Builds on: engineering-rigor-at-speed lesson 3 (you own every line) and lesson 8 (writing that scales).

## The problem and why it matters

Two scenes.

**Scene one: your own portfolio repo.** You build a project with an AI agent, put it on GitHub, and link it from your resume. A hiring engineer opens it. Do the commit dates match what you claim? Does the README say what the AI did? Can you explain the design in an interview without the tool? The repo is evidence. If it overclaims, one question collapses it.

**Scene two: someone else's project.** You find a bug in a popular library, ask an agent for a fix, and open a pull request (PR: a proposed change to someone else's repo). The maintainer (the person who reviews and merges) opens it, sees 300 lines they cannot tell you understand, and has 40 other PRs waiting. They are volunteers. Your PR costs their time, and they now have to guess how much of it a person thought about.

Both scenes are about trust, and trust is about an honest, checkable record.

## First principles

1. **A public repo is a claim, so keep claims checkable.** Dates, numbers and "I built this" statements should have evidence behind them (commit history, saved run output).
2. **Disclosure is cheap and its absence is expensive.** One sentence of "an AI tool drafted this; I reviewed it" costs nothing. Being found out later costs a lot.
3. **Maintainer time is the scarce resource in open source.** Your job is to reduce their effort, not hand them an unread diff.
4. **Each project sets its own rules.** Policies on AI vary from "disclose" to "do not use". Read the project's own page; never assume.
5. **You must be able to defend every line.** If you cannot explain it without the tool, do not submit it.
6. **A signed, small-step history is a record nobody can fake later.** Squashing a project into one commit erases the evidence of how you worked.

## How it works

### Project policies differ, so read theirs first

Three real policies, read on their own pages on 2026-10-29. Policies change; check the live page before you contribute.

```
 QEMU           declines contributions
 (emulator)     believed to include AI-
                generated content
 Linux kernel   allowed with disclosure and
 (docs)         extra scrutiny; you must be
                able to defend it
 Ghostty        all AI use disclosed; tool
 (terminal)     and extent named; human must
                understand all code
```

What each page says (text in quotation marks is verbatim from the page; the rest is my paraphrase):

- **QEMU** (code provenance page): "Current QEMU project policy is to DECLINE any contributions which are believed to include or derive from AI generated content." The page names ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot and Llama, and says it will decline a contribution "if use of AI is either known or suspected". It says the policy "does not apply to other uses of AI, such as researching APIs or algorithms, static analysis, or debugging, provided their output is not included in contributions." Exceptions are discussed on the project's mailing list. Every patch needs a `Signed-off-by:` line, which certifies you have the right to submit it under the project's license (the Developer's Certificate of Origin, DCO).
- **Linux kernel** (generated-content page): "These guidelines apply when a meaningful amount of content in a kernel contribution was not written by a person". It asks contributors to "be transparent about the origin of content in cover letters and changelogs" (my paraphrase of the detail: which tools, their inputs, what they affected, how it was tested). It says to "expect additional scrutiny in proportion to how much of it was generated" and "You are expected to understand and to be able to defend everything you submit." It names no required tag or trailer format. (A *cover letter* is the introductory email that goes with a series of patches.)
- **Ghostty** (`AI_POLICY.md`): "All AI usage in any form must be disclosed" (naming the tool and the extent of AI assistance). "The human-in-the-loop must fully understand all code." "No AI-generated media is allowed (art, images, videos, audio, etc.)." "People who produce bad contributions that are clearly AI (slop) will be added to our public denouncement list." "Maintainers are exempt from these rules and may use AI tools at their discretion"

The contrast is the lesson. The same agent-written patch is welcome with a note in one project and refused in another. "It is legal" or "other projects accept it" is no argument. Their repo, their rules.

### Contribution etiquette with AI

```
 before you write anything
   │ read CONTRIBUTING + the AI policy
   │ search issues: is it known / claimed?
   ▼
 open or comment on an issue first
   │ say what you plan, wait for a nod
   ▼
 small PR, one concern, tests included
   │ you ran it; you can explain it
   ▼
 PR text: what, why, how checked,
   AI use disclosed in their format
   ▼
 respond to review yourself, not by
 pasting the reviewer's words to a bot
```

Rules I follow (heuristics from experience, not measurements):

- **Ask first on anything bigger than a typo.** A surprise 800-line PR is a burden even when it is good.
- **One concern per PR.** Do not mix a fix, a rename and a reformat.
- **Reproduce the bug yourself** and show it in the PR (command and output). An agent's guess at a cause is not a reproduction.
- **Follow local style.** Run the project's formatter and linter. Match tests to its test style.
- **Do not paste the tool's explanation as your description.** Write two or three sentences in your own words. If you cannot, you do not understand the change yet.
- **Answer review comments with your own judgement.** Maintainers are talking to you.
- **Do not use an agent to mass-file issues or PRs.** It multiplies the cost to the maintainer, not to you.
- **Accept "no" quickly.** A rejection for policy reasons is not personal.

### The maintainer's burden

Review is slow, unpaid and the bottleneck. AI changed the arithmetic: writing a plausible patch got cheaper, reading one did not. A reasonable response from a maintainer is a policy like the ones above. If you maintain a project yourself, your first useful step is a short written policy (what must be disclosed, what is banned, what happens on a violation). One clear page beats case-by-case arguments.

### Disclosing in a commit or PR

Common, simple options (choose per project; none is a universal standard):

```text
Fix off-by-one in retry loop

Reproduced with `make test T=retry`; failed before,
passes after.

Assisted-by: <tool name> (drafted patch; I rewrote
the test and verified on real input)
Signed-off-by: Your Name <you@example.com>
```

- `Signed-off-by:` is a DCO convention that some projects require, such as QEMU. It is about legal right to submit, not about AI.
- `Assisted-by:` here is my own wording, not a standard. Use whatever the project asks for. If the project names a format, use that.
- Claude Code has settings that control the attribution it adds to commits and PR descriptions: `attribution.commit` and `attribution.pr` (names from the settings index fetched 2026-10-29; `includeCoAuthoredBy` is deprecated). I did not verify the defaults. Do not strip attribution on your own repos just to look more independent. Keep it accurate.

### Keeping an honest record on your own repos

You want the history to answer three questions: when did this happen, what did the AI do, what did I do.

1. **Small, meaningful commits.** Never squash a whole feature into one. The dated history is the evidence.
2. **Signed commits.** A signature shows the commit came from a key you control. GitHub (fetched 2026-10-29) accepts GPG, SSH or S/MIME signing; SSH is described as the simplest. A "Verified" badge means the signature was checked. Never turn signing off to get past an error; fix the key.
3. **Numbers only from saved runs.** If a README says "3x faster", a file in the repo holds the command, raw output and hardware. Otherwise leave the number out.
4. **A decisions and failures log.** After each decision, experiment or dead end, add a dated line: what was tried, what happened, what you chose. Keep the failures; they are the strongest evidence you really did the work.
5. **An accurate "How this was built" section** in the README: which tools, for what, what you wrote or checked yourself.
6. **Consistency across places.** Resume, site, profile and READMEs must agree on every date and number. If they disagree, fix the source of truth first.

### Runnable demo: a signed commit with a disclosure trailer

A *trailer* is a `Key: value` line at the end of a commit message. This runs in a throwaway repo with a throwaway SSH key, ignoring your global git config, so it touches nothing of yours. The steps were:

```bash
export GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL=/dev/null GIT_CONFIG_SYSTEM=/dev/null
git init -q -b main . && git config user.email demo@example.com
ssh-keygen -q -t ed25519 -N "" -C demo -f "$T/key"
echo "demo@example.com $(cut -d' ' -f1,2 "$T/key.pub")" > "$T/allowed_signers"
git config gpg.format ssh
git config user.signingkey "$T/key.pub"
git config gpg.ssh.allowedSignersFile "$T/allowed_signers"
git config commit.gpgsign true
git commit -m "Add a.txt" \
  -m "Assisted-by: example-agent (drafted; I reviewed and edited)"
git log -1 --show-signature
git log -1 --format='%h %G?'
git log -1 --format=%B | git interpret-trailers --parse
```

Real output on this macOS machine:

```text
commit bd94d817149f68009d5f38cd68ebc9c749cd2bf5
Good "git" signature for demo@example.com with ED25519 key SHA256:TIjN6m...
Author: t <demo@example.com>
bd94d81 G
Assisted-by: example-agent (drafted; I reviewed and edited)
```

(The first three lines are `git log -1 --show-signature` cut to its first three lines; hashes and key fingerprints differ on every run.) A second commit made on purpose with signing switched off for that one command (`git -c commit.gpgsign=false commit`) showed status `N` (no signature) in `git log --format='%h %G? %s'`:

```text
a0af0c4 N unsigned
bd94d81 G Add a.txt
34e67d6 N base
```

(`base` was made before signing was configured, so it is also `N`.) The status letter `G` means a good signature, `N` none. That `%G?` check is what a script or a CI job (automatic checks on a PR) would use to find unsigned commits in a range. For your real repo, follow GitHub's docs to upload your signing key; I did not run that here.

### AI-record template for a personal repo

Put this in `docs/journal.md` or similar. Keep it short and dated:

```markdown
## 2026-10-29: retry loop
- Tried: asked the agent for a backoff fix.
- Result: it passed its own test; my replay of
  the real failing input still failed.
- Decided: wrote the failing test myself first,
  agent implemented, I rewrote the edge case.
- AI did: draft code. I did: test, review, run.
```

The record is not for show. Future you will forget which part you understood, and an interviewer will ask.

### Using an AI tool on someone else's code safely

- Read their `CONTRIBUTING` and AI policy before opening the tool.
- Do not paste private or embargoed material (security reports, unreleased code) into a tool without the owner's agreement.
- Check any new dependency the tool suggests exists and is maintained (engineering-rigor-at-speed lesson 3).
- Check the license of anything it copies in. A tool can reproduce code it saw in training. Whether that is a problem is a legal question I am not qualified to answer; when in doubt, write it yourself.

## Common mistakes

- Opening a large AI-written PR without discussing it first.
- Not disclosing, then being asked "did a tool write this?" in review.
- Disclosing to a project that bans AI content, then arguing about it.
- Squashing everything into one commit "to tidy the history".
- Quoting a benchmark number from memory instead of a saved run.
- Letting the README say "built by hand" or "fully AI-built" when neither is exactly true.
- Using the tool to answer reviewers instead of thinking.
- Disabling commit signing to get past a key error.

## Try it

15-20 minutes:

1. Pick one open-source project you use. Find its `CONTRIBUTING` file and look for any AI or generated-content policy. Write the rule in one sentence of your own words, or write "none found".
2. In a scratch repo, run the demo steps with a throwaway key. Confirm `%G?` prints `G`, then make an unsigned commit and confirm `N`.
3. Write the three-bullet "How this was built" section for one of your repos, truthfully.
4. Draft a PR description for a real fix you could make: what, why, how checked, AI use. Keep it under 120 words.

## Checklist (one page)

- [ ] I read the project's contributing guide and AI policy before starting.
- [ ] I opened or commented on an issue first for anything non-trivial.
- [ ] My PR is small, one concern, with tests.
- [ ] I reproduced the bug and ran the fix myself.
- [ ] I can explain every line without the tool.
- [ ] I disclosed AI use in the format the project asks for.
- [ ] I did not paste secrets or embargoed material into a tool.
- [ ] On my repos: small signed commits, no squashing, signing never disabled.
- [ ] Every number in a README has a saved run behind it, with hardware named.
- [ ] A dated journal records decisions, failures and who did what.
- [ ] README "How this was built" is accurate; resume, site and READMEs agree.

## First week plan

- Day 1: choose one repo of yours as the showcase; list every claim in its README and mark which have evidence.
- Day 2: set up commit signing; verify a test commit shows Verified on GitHub.
- Day 3: start the journal; backfill what you remember, marked as written later.
- Day 4: pick a target open-source project; read its guidelines; find one small issue and comment that you are looking at it.
- Day 5: make the fix with tests, disclose per the project's rules, open the PR, and stay available for review.

## Sources

Fetched this session (2026-10-29). Policy pages were read through a page-reading tool; quotes above are as it returned them. Read the live page before relying on any wording.

- https://www.qemu.org/docs/master/devel/code-provenance.html: QEMU AI-content policy and Signed-off-by/DCO requirement.
- https://docs.kernel.org/process/generated-content.html: Linux kernel guidance on tool-generated content (scope, transparency, scrutiny, no required tag format).
- https://github.com/ghostty-org/ghostty/blob/main/AI_POLICY.md: Ghostty AI policy (disclosure, media ban, understanding, denouncement list, maintainer exemption).
- https://docs.github.com/en/authentication/managing-commit-signature-verification/about-commit-signature-verification: GPG/SSH/S/MIME signing, what Verified means.
- https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference: names of the attribution keys (defaults not read).
- https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/managing-protected-branches/about-protected-branches: "require signed commits" option.

Not verified: the attribution keys' defaults; licensing questions about generated code; any project policy not listed above; uploading a signing key to GitHub (not run).
